text: The last two lessons showed you raw new and delete, and the two ways they go wrong: forget the delete and you leak memory, use the pointer afterward and you get undefined behavior. Modern C++ almost never calls new and delete directly anymore. This lesson is about why.

The pattern that makes that possible is called RAII. Acquire a resource — memory, a file, a socket, a lock — in a constructor, and release it in the destructor. Because C++ guarantees that destructor runs the instant the object goes out of scope, even when an exception is thrown through that scope, the resource always gets released. You never have to remember to clean up by hand. A smart pointer is simply RAII applied to heap memory.

This is what that looks like for a single owned object. The unique pointer owns the Order, and the instant it goes out of scope, its destructor automatically calls delete for you. Notice the function used to create it — prefer make_unique over calling new directly; it's exception-safe and slightly more concise.

unique_ptr is your default smart pointer, and for good reason. It can't be copied — only moved, which you'll learn properly in lesson ten — because copying it would mean two owners of the same object, which defeats the whole point. It has zero runtime overhead compared to a raw pointer; it's purely a compile-time safety wrapper. And it deletes the object automatically the moment it goes out of scope.

Sometimes ownership genuinely needs to be shared, and that's what shared_ptr is for. Multiple shared pointers can own the same object at once, tracked by an internal reference count you can even inspect. The object is only actually freed once the last owner is gone. That flexibility isn't free — there's a reference count to maintain — so reach for it only when sharing is a real requirement.

A few habits keep all of this safe. Default to unique_ptr, and reach for shared_ptr only when ownership is genuinely shared. Prefer make_unique and make_shared over calling new yourself. And never manually delete an object a smart pointer already owns — that's a double-free waiting to happen.

RAII ties cleanup to an object's lifetime so it happens automatically, and unique_ptr and shared_ptr apply that to heap memory so raw new and delete should almost never appear in your code again. Up next, lesson nine: memory bugs and sanitizers, where you'll learn to actually find it when these rules get broken.
